title: Xiaomi's Three Chips at Once: Trading Resources for Time, Betting on a Paradigm Shift in On-Device AI
dek: Xiaomi released three Xuanjie chips in one go, aggressively betting on memory interconnect, 3D stacking and an all-AI architecture — trading resources for time, wagering on a paradigm shift in on-device AI and vertical integration, though a clear gap remains to the top chip companies.
why: This deep-dive parses the technical choices and strategic logic behind Xiaomi's three chips with high information density, especially the clear analogies for key technologies like memory interconnect and 3D stacking. Worth a listen for chip industry professionals and investors watching Xiaomi.
who: Investors following Xiaomi's chip efforts, chip industry engineers, product managers, and tech professionals who want to understand the on-device AI trend.
skip: The first 3 minutes of discussion about the definition of in-house development can be skipped; go straight to the technical analysis.

points.h: Whether a company can make chips depends on system definition rights, not IP self-sufficiency rate
points.body: Judging whether a company can make chips is not about how many IP blocks it hand-built, but about how much system definition rights it holds. Although Xiaomi's Xuanjie O1 uses ARM IP for CPU and GPU, the system integration and physical implementation are its own. Apple and Qualcomm are strong because they can iterate every year and keep taping out — exactly what latecomers lack most. Xiaomi doesn't have ten years to learn slowly, so it chose an aggressive route, pushing multiple high-risk technology lines at once.

points.h: The culprit behind O1's poor efficiency is the lack of a shared water tank
points.body: Xuanjie O1 has no system-level cache (SLC), so GPU power draw can't be contained under high load and efficiency suffers. SLC is like a shared water tank for a neighborhood: the closer data is to the compute unit, the faster the access and the lower the power. O1's GPU has many cores but limited DDR bandwidth, so many cores sit waiting for data and utilization stays low — this is the bandwidth wall. O3 adds 16MB of SLC, splits it into multiple cache blocks distributed across the chip, and designs an on-chip network scheduling system to resolve data consistency and access conflicts.

points.h: ARM's public bus is too generic, so Xuanjie had to build its own
points.body: ARM's public CHI+CMN scheme is too generic, requiring compatibility and redundancy designs that are hard to customize for Xuanjie. O3 simply developed its own X-Ring unified converged bus, compatible with CHI but defining its own interconnect protocol, along with a self-developed high-speed road network scheduling center and memory controller. This means fewer protocol conversions, and data can decide cache location and path based on need. Xiaomi's data claims protocol conversion overhead is reduced by 75%, static access latency is 82 nanoseconds, 32% lower than O1, and even lower than Apple's A19 Pro.

points.h: The compute bottleneck is shifting from matrix multiplication to vector operations
points.body: O3 adds an AI unit to every subsystem — CPU, GPU, ISP and more — so computation happens where the data is, reducing data movement. The NPU core count drops from 6 to 4, but Tensor compute rises to 200Tops, because Xiaomi judges that the large-model bottleneck is expanding from matrix multiplication to vector operations such as Softmax, quantization and KVCache. The vector unit's area is about the same as Tensor's, its multiply-accumulate units are 6.8 times O1's, and it introduces an SMT-like architecture, similar to CUDA, to handle irregular parallel tasks.

points.h: Chips and models should be defined together by the same company
points.body: Xiaomi worked with MEMO to compress INT4 weights to 5 bits using a 5-value quantization method, with almost no precision loss and a 30% reduction in memory bandwidth and capacity requirements. The 3-billion-parameter MEMO model deployed on O3 improves prefill performance by 40% and decode by 45%. This ability to jointly define chip and model is the closed-loop advantage of vertical integration — no need to wait for someone else to define a model and then adapt.

points.h: 3nm performance is squeezed out bit by bit from standard cells
points.body: O3 uses the more mature N3P process, gaining 5% performance at the same power and 5%-10% lower power at the same frequency. Xiaomi also did extensive process optimization: self-developed standard cells increased from 480 on O1 to over 2,400, covering every unit of the chip; by compressing the power supply buffer channel so power and signals run through the middle of the module, transistor density rises 5%. The CPU moves from 4 clusters to 3 clusters of 10 all-big cores, with single-core performance up 31% and multi-core up 60%, surpassing A19 Pro.

points.h: Near-memory computing pushes phone memory bandwidth to 1.22TB/s
points.body: Xuanjie O100 uses wafer-level 3D stacking: one compute wafer plus two memory wafers stacked vertically, interconnected via Hybrid Bonding to form a near-memory computing architecture. It uses thousands of shorter, denser vertical connections to achieve high bandwidth, with lower energy per bit shifted — like HBM on a phone. The data: 28,762 data connections, 1.22TB/s bandwidth, far exceeding the tens-of-bits-wide connections of traditional SoC and LPDDR. The compute layer has 14 independent cores, each paired with a RISC-V processor for control.

points.h: ChangXin's value isn't in the speed grade, it's in joint definition
points.body: Xiaomi partnered with ChangXin for the first launch of LPDDR6, reducing dependence on Samsung and SK Hynix. Even if ChangXin provides a starting grade of 10.667Gbps, Xiaomi can compensate for the peak rate gap through wider channels, larger SLC and a self-developed memory controller. More importantly, the two sides jointly verify and tune from the design stage, jointly defining a mobile memory subsystem solution for China. For ChangXin, it proves its high-speed IO and physical layer capabilities and seats it at the table for the new generation of mobile memory.

points.h: What Xiaomi is betting on isn't chips, it's a time window
points.body: First, it bets on a paradigm shift in on-device computing: AI carries increasing weight in the SoC, the phone becomes the AI interaction entry point, and Xiaomi wants to stand as the definer. Second, it bets that vertical integration becomes the core competitiveness of terminal companies: general-purpose chips can hardly meet the fragmented needs of the full phone-car-home scenario, so it must control its own compute architecture. Third, it bets on an uncertain time window, trading resources for time, compressing the technology catch-up cycle — willing to bear engineering risk rather than wait for the window to close.

points.h: Xuanjie is catching up faster, but it hasn't cleared any of the three thresholds
points.body: A top SoC company needs three capabilities: self-developed CPU/GPU microarchitecture, a self-developed 5G baseband, and stable tape-outs across multiple consecutive generations with tens-of-millions shipments. Xuanjie currently satisfies none of them, and a clear gap remains to the first tier — it is only catching up faster. What truly changes the industry landscape is not one stunning chip, but the sustained iteration capability built by a group of companies. Xuanjie's greater significance is proving Xiaomi's chip effort hasn't stopped, and that it is starting to move forward together with Chinese chip industry partners.

terms.def: A cache shared by multiple compute units within a chip, like a shared water tank for a neighborhood.
A wafer-level 3D stacking interconnect technology that connects directly through copper pillars, with high bandwidth and low power.
Placing memory close to compute units to reduce data movement distance and improve bandwidth and energy efficiency.
When data movement capability becomes the performance bottleneck, no amount of compute cores can help.
A parallel processing architecture that can manage multiple task groups at once, improving compute unit utilization.

quotes.text: Judging whether a company can really make chips, you shouldn't just stare at how many IP blocks it hand-built — you should look at how much system definition rights it holds.
Xiaomi isn't slowly learning to make chips; it's trading resources for time, building up as fast as possible the complete capability station a mature chip company needs within a limited time window.
As long as data is stored sensibly and delivered efficiently, the entire chip benefits.
Once it's done, there's no need to wait for someone else's defined model, then adapt a general-purpose chip to it, and then figure out how to cram it into a phone.
I'd rather bear more engineering and R&D uncertainty than wait until the window truly closes and regret not having moved a few steps faster.
